docs.title: Linear Regression
docs.text: Linear regression is one of the simplest and most widely used machine learning techniques. It models the relationship between an input variable (or several inputs) and an output variable by fitting a straight line (or hyperplane) through the data.

docs.title: The Equation
docs.text:
For a single input variable \( x \), the model is:

\[ y = w x + b \]
  • \( y \) → predicted output
  • \( x \) → input variable
  • \( w \) → weight (slope of the line)
  • \( b \) → bias (intercept)

For multiple input variables:

\[ y = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_n x_n + b \]

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Inputs: numerical data (e.g., beam length, load, temperature).
  • Outputs: a predicted continuous value (e.g., deflection, stress, efficiency).
  • Goal: find the best line (or hyperplane) that minimizes the difference between predicted and actual values.

docs.title: Engineering Applications
docs.text:
• Predicting material properties (e.g., tensile strength vs. composition).
  • Estimating drag coefficient from geometry.
  • Correlating beam deflection with load and length.

Note

Linear regression is often used as a baseline model. If it performs well, more complex machine learning models may not be needed.

docs.title: The Essence of Machine Learning
docs.text:
Let’s begin with a simple but powerful idea — learning relationships from data.

Take a classic engineering example: the linear stress–strain relationship

\[ \sigma = E \, \varepsilon \]

where \( E \) is the elastic modulus. In theory, this line is perfectly straight — but in practice, experimental sensors introduce noise, so our data looks more like this:

Now, suppose we want to determine the true value of \( E \) (the gradient of the line) from this noisy data. A common approach is to use linear regression, which finds the best-fitting line

\[ y = m x + c \]

by minimizing the difference between the model’s predictions and the measured data.

docs.title: Measuring error — Mean Squared Error (MSE)
docs.text:
We define an error function that quantifies how far off our model is from the real data:

\[ \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i - (m x_i + c) \right)^2 \]

This computes the average of the squared differences between the measured values \( y_i \) and our model’s predictions \( \hat{y}_i = m x_i + c \). Our goal is to find the parameters \( m \) and \( c \) that minimize this error.

docs.title: Learning from error — Gradient Descent
docs.text:
To improve the model, we compute how the error changes with respect to each parameter:

[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial m} = -\frac{2}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i (y_i - \hat{y}i) ] [ \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = -\frac{2}{N} \sum_i) ]}^{N} (y_i - \hat{y

These are called gradients — they tell us the direction in which to adjust each parameter to reduce the error.

We then update the parameters iteratively:

[ m \leftarrow m - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial m} ] [ c \leftarrow c - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} ]

where \( \eta \) (eta) is the learning rate, controlling how big each step is.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
And that — in essence — is machine learning. Every algorithm, from linear regression to deep neural networks, follows the same fundamental idea:

  1. Make a prediction
  2. Measure how wrong it is
  3. Adjust the model to reduce that error

The models may become vastly more complex, but underneath it all lies the same principle: continuous optimization using differential error signals to approach an optimal solution.

docs.title: What is Machine Learning?
docs.text:
The human brain is an incredibly good pattern detector. Take face recognition as an example - it's second nature to humans, yet you (probably) were never told how to recognise people. Even if you meet thousands of people in your lifetime, with features that can change over time and are likely not too dissimilar to each other, you can still easily recognise people.

Now imagine being asked to program this ability into a computer with traditional coding techniques - meaning defining explicit features like measuring nose shape, jaw structure, hair colours etc. You'd have to decide on a huge number of variables to measure and even then the program would likely struggle when photo conditions are different.

Machine Learning techniques in constrast learn the key features in data which contribute to the results. We never tell the computer how to learn, yet through feedback it is able to arrive at the correct result.

docs.title: Why should Engineers use Machine Learning?
docs.text:
The above concept is a hugely powerful one, since if we don't need to create rules, the computer can learn new rules/features just based on its internal reward system. Engineering often involves huge amounts of data and complex system dynamics - an environment where ML methods can outperform traditional approaches.

ML can handle an array of engineering problems from design optimisation, fault detection and control systems.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
For now, we will just categorise types of Machine learning by their architecture - that is, what information do they learn with.

  • Supervised Learning - Inputs and Results are given to the model and it learns to map inputs

    • Prediction and Classification
    • Regression, Neural Networks

  • Unsupervised Learning - Results not given to the model, and the model is tasked with finding patterns on its own

    • Feature Engineering, Clustering
    • k-means clustering, Autoencoders

  • Reinforcement Learning - Model interacts with an environment using trial and error

    • Control policies
    • Q-learning, Proximal Policy Optimisation

docs.title: Machine Learning for Engineers, not data scientists
docs.text:
Machine Learning has huge untapped potential in engineering problems, and we believe the piece of the puzzle missing is that good ML models require domain knowledge, something only engineers can provide.

We aim for this site to become an open-source wiki page designed to minimise time to ML production for engineers to gain useful insights into complex systems.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Although the site functions as a library and can be read in any order, beginners are encouraged to follow the sections in sequence to build a complete foundation before starting their own projects.

Contributions to the wiki can be made through our GitHub repository . In the future, we plan to expand the site with a community forum and a blog for user-submitted projects and tutorials, however for now feel free to direct any questions on the Github discussion board.

docs.title: Books
docs.text:
• Approaching machine learning problems in computational fluid dynamics and computer aided engineering applications: A Monograph for Beginners - Dr Justin Hodges - A crash course in ML integration in engineering, easy to read.
  • Data-Driven Science and Engineering - J. Nathan Kutz and Steven L. Brunton - A deep dive into the maths used in scientific ML with lots of applied code. Steve's Youtube Channel also a great resource
  • Hands on Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow - Aurelien Geron - Implementations for almost any ML model you might need

docs.title: Lectures
docs.text:
• Stanford CS231N - Computer Vision Lecture Series but also offers great intuition of architectures
  • ETH Zürich | AI in the Sciences and Engineering - Focus on Physics-Based ML architectures

docs.title: About the creator
docs.text:
Joel Corbishley is an Aerospace Engineer with a Master’s degree from the University of Leeds, specialising in Computational Fluid Dynamics and Machine Learning in Engineering. He has hands-on experience in aerodynamic design, structural analysis and simulation development and has led multiple academic and industrial research projects in these areas.

The project grew out of a realisation that many engineers are curious about machine learning but are discouraged by the mathematical depth of most resources. Engineering ML Wiki focuses on a results-driven hands-on approach, emphasising real-world workflows, reproducible examples, and collaboration.

He is currently open to opportunities in software, simulation, or applied ML.
